en: The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter One: Inquiry into Matters. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as innumerable multitudes of devas, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others; all were seated together in the great assembly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to ask a question; if you will grant me leave, I shall now inquire."
The Buddha said: “Excellent!
Ask whatever you wish; I shall now explain it for you.”
Bhadra asked the Buddha:
"By practicing what dharmas does a bodhisattva attain wisdom, such that it gathers all streams like the great ocean?
How should they practice so as to be extensively proficient in all knowledge, understanding everything they hear without doubt?"
By what practice does one come to know one's own past lives and where one has come from?
By what practice does one attain a long life?
By what practice is one always born into a great clan, such that one's parents, brothers, kinsmen, and friends all love and respect one?
By what practice does one obtain a countenance that is upright, handsome, and exquisitely beautiful?
By what means does one attain lofty talent that far surpasses the masses, with wisdom so penetrating that there is nothing it does not encompass?
By what practice does one establish merit, fulfill the marks, and personally attain Buddhahood with immeasurable majestic power, such that the realm of a Buddha is adorned with a magnificent land?
By what practice does one subdue the enmity of Māra?
By what practice does one attain mastery such that one's vows are never thwarted?
By what practice does one enter the gateways of dhāraṇī?
By what practice does one attain the supernormal powers to travel everywhere throughout all Buddha-lands?
By practicing what conduct does one attain a valor like that of a lion, remaining fearless so that no māras can move one?
By practicing what conduct does one attain the noble nature of a Buddha, receiving and upholding all sūtras and dharmas, understanding them all thoroughly without forgetting?
By what practice does one attain self-sufficiency, become free from flattery and deceit, and remain unattached to the three spheres?
By what practice does one attain freedom from hindrance, uphold the teachings of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), and never lose the Buddha’s intent?
By what practice does one gain the trust of people?
By what practice does one attain the eightfold voice that enters into ten trillion sounds?
By what practice does one attain the complete marks and signs of excellence?
By what practice does one attain the power of hearing all things?
By what practice does one attain the eye of the Path to perceive the future?
By what practice does one attain the ten powers and the correct, true wisdom?
How should one practice so that the minds of all Buddhas of the ten directions appear before one through a single moment of mindfulness?
How should one practice so as to know that the four bases are fundamentally non-existent?

How should one practice so that, while remaining in this very place, one sees the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and thoroughly understands the destinies of good and evil for the people therein—including humans, devas, nāgas, spirits, and even the wriggling insects?
"Since the questions asked are thus, how should one practice?
We pray that the Buddha will explain this to resolve all doubts.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Excellent! That which you have asked transcends all bounds and cannot be calculated.

That you are able to pose such a question is due to the merit you cultivated during the time of past Buddhas in previous lives—by making offerings to those Buddhas, delighting in the Dharma, and maintaining the observance of the precepts with purity."

It is because they constantly practice begging for alms rather than accepting invitations; because they frequently bring about the assemblies of various bodhisattvas; because they teach and exhort others to abandon all evils; because they regard all things with complete equanimity;
and because they always possess great loving-kindness and great compassion.
"Your merit is beyond further calculation.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"There is a samādhi called 'All Buddhas of the Ten Directions Standing Before One. If one can practice this dharma, everything you have asked about can be attained."
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We pray that you will explain this for us.
What the Buddha now speaks will deliver many and bring peace and security to the ten directions, manifesting the signs of great illumination for all bodhisattvas.”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"There is a samādhi called 'concentrated mind' (samāhita-citta), which a bodhisattva should constantly guard, practice, and maintain. One must not again follow other dharmas; this is the foremost among all merits."
2. Chapter on Practice, Second. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to quickly attain this samādhi, they must always establish great faith; if they practice in accordance with the Dharma, they shall obtain it."
Do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of doubt; this method of meditative concentration is called "the Bodhisattva’s Transcendence of All Practices.
Establish a single thought, Believe in this Dharma, And according to what you have heard, Mindfully direct your attention toward that source.
One should maintain single-minded focus, sever all discursive thoughts, establish firm faith, and harbor no doubts;
practice with diligence and never be indolent.
Do not give rise to the notion of existence or non-existence;
do not think of advancing, nor think of retreating;
do not think of the front, nor think of the back.
Do not think of the left, do not think of the right;
do not think of non-existence, do not think of existence;
do not think of the distant, do not think of the near.
Do not dwell on pain; do not dwell on itching;
do not dwell on hunger; do not dwell on thirst;
do not dwell on cold; do not dwell on heat.
Do not dwell on suffering, nor dwell on pleasure;
do not dwell on birth, nor dwell on old age, nor dwell on sickness,
nor dwell on death.
Do not dwell on the body; do not dwell on life; do not dwell on longevity.
Do not dwell on poverty; do not dwell on wealth.
Do not dwell on nobility; do not dwell on lowliness.
Do not dwell on form; do not dwell on desire;
do not dwell on the small; do not dwell on the large;
do not dwell on the long; do not dwell on the short.
Do not dwell on the beautiful, nor dwell on the ugly;
do not dwell on the evil, nor dwell on the good;
do not dwell on anger, nor dwell on joy.
Do not think of sitting, do not think of rising;
do not think of walking, do not think of standing;
do not think of the sutras, do not think of the Dharma.
Do not dwell on what is right, nor dwell on what is wrong;
do not dwell on renunciation, nor dwell on grasping;
do not dwell on perception, nor dwell on consciousness.
Do not dwell on annihilation, nor dwell on attachment;
do not dwell on emptiness, nor dwell on reality;
do not dwell on lightness, nor dwell on heaviness.
Do not dwell on what is difficult, nor dwell on what is easy;
do not dwell on what is deep, nor dwell on what is shallow;
do not dwell on what is vast, nor dwell on what is narrow.
Do not think of your father; do not think of your mother;
do not think of your wife; do not think of your son;
do not think of your kin; do not think of those who are distant.
Do not dwell on hatred, do not dwell on love;
do not dwell on gain, do not dwell on loss;
do not dwell on success, do not dwell on failure.
Do not dwell on purity, do not dwell on impurity.
Cut off all thoughts; for this single moment of thought, let the mind not be distracted, but remain constantly diligent.
Do not be indolent; do not calculate by the year; do not grow weary by the day.
Establish a single thought-moment and do not neglect it midway; cast off sleep and refine your intention.
Always dwell alone and do not gather in crowds;
avoid evil people and draw near to virtuous friends;
rely upon an enlightened teacher and regard them as a Buddha.
Maintain this resolve, always remaining gentle and pliant; contemplate equality toward all things.
Avoid one's hometown and distance oneself from kinsmen.
Abandoning craving and desire, tread the path of purity.
Practice non-action and sever all cravings.
Cast off distracted thoughts and cultivate the practice of meditative concentration.
One who studies the wisdom of letters must be like one in meditation.
Eliminate the three impurities and abandon the six sense bases.
Sever lustful desire and detach from all sensations.
Do not covet wealth, nor hoard it in great quantities.
Be content with food; do not crave its flavors.
Regarding the lives of sentient beings, be careful never to eat them.
Wear robes in accordance with the Dharma; do not adorn them with finery.
Do not engage in frivolous play; do not be arrogant.
Do not be conceited; do not be haughty.
If you preach the sutras, you should do so in accordance with the Dharma.
Realize that the body is fundamentally like an illusion.
Do not grasp at the aggregates; do not enter the sense-spheres.
The aggregates are like thieves; the four elements are like snakes.
They are impermanent and elusive; they have no permanent master, for their fundamental nature is non-existent.
Conditions meet, and conditions disperse; understanding all this, one knows they are fundamentally non-existent.
Extend compassion and pity toward all beings.
Bestowing gifts upon the poor and aiding those who do not repay—
this is the certainty of the bodhisattva’s practice;
it is the essential wisdom that gives rise to all forms of knowledge.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"By practicing these dharmas, one will immediately attain samādhi, and all the Buddhas of the present will stand before one.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who practice according to the Dharma and maintain their precepts in their entirety, dwelling alone in a secluded place, they should bring to mind Amitābha Buddha of the West, who exists at this very moment. According to what they have heard, they should keep him in mind; he resides in a land called Sukhāvatī, ten billion million buddha-fields away from here."
Focus your mind on this for one day and night, or seven days and seven nights. After the seven days have passed, you will see it.

It is like what one sees in a dream: one does not know day from night, nor does one know inside from outside; it is not because one is in darkness or because there is something obscuring or obstructing that one does not see.
Bhadra! A bodhisattva should form this thought:

"At that time, within the realms of all Buddha-lands, wherever there are great mountains or Mount Sumerus, and whatever places are dark and obscure, they shall all be opened up and made free from obstruction."

This bodhisattva does not employ the divine eye to see through, nor the divine ear to hear through, nor does he travel to that buddha-field by means of the power of psychic travel; rather, without passing away from this place to be born in that place, he beholds it while sitting right here.

For example, suppose a person hears that in the kingdom of Śrāvastī there is a courtesan named Sumanā; another person hears of a courtesan named Āmrapālī; and yet another hears that Upavartana has also become a courtesan.

At that time, although these people have never seen these three women, their lustful thoughts are immediately stirred upon hearing of them. These three individuals, all residing in the city of Rājagṛha, simultaneously form these thoughts and each, in a dream, arrives at the side of the woman, stays with her for the night, and upon waking, each remembers her.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"I employ these three women as a metaphor; you should take this matter and preach the sūtra for others, so that they may understand this wisdom and reach the stage of non-retrogression on the path to unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment."
"If you later attain Buddhahood, your name shall be 'Well-Awakened' (Sujāta).
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva in this world-system contemplates Amitābha Buddha, by virtue of such single-minded contemplation, they shall behold him."
He then asked:
"By practicing what Dharma can one be born in this land?
Amitābha Buddha replied:
"Those who wish to be born hereafter should constantly recite my name without ceasing, and they shall attain rebirth there.
The Buddha said:

"By means of single-minded recollection, one attains rebirth in that land. One should constantly contemplate the Buddha’s body as possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, with billions of rays of light shining through all, its sublime form being peerless, preaching the Dharma amidst the assembly of Bodhisattvas without changing its color."

Why is this? Because by means of mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains this samādhi, which is indestructible regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, the soul (ātman), earth, water, fire, and wind, and extends throughout the world, including the heavens up to the Brahmā and Mahābrahmā realms.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Who can bear witness to this samādhi of the bodhisattva?
My disciples Mahākāśyapa, Indradatta, and the Devaputra Susīma, as well as those who understand it in a timely manner and have attained it through practice—they are the witnesses."
In this way, Bhadrapāla!

Those who wish to see the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions should single-mindedly focus their thoughts on those quarters and harbor no other thoughts; in this manner, they shall be able to see them.
It is like a person who has traveled far away to another region or kingdom and longs for his native village, his home, and his kinsmen;
that person returns to his native village in a dream, sees his family and relatives, and joyfully converses with them, and upon waking, recounts it thus to his friends.
The Buddha said:
“If a bodhisattva hears the name of a buddha and wishes to see him, by constantly keeping that direction in mind, they shall immediately behold him.

It is like a bhikṣu contemplating the bones of a dead person placed before him; at times they appear blue, at times white, at times red, and at times black. These colors do not come from anywhere else; they are merely what the mind conceives.”

In this way, the bodhisattva, upholding the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, establishes mastery within samādhi; whichever direction’s buddha they wish to see, they immediately behold them. Why is this?
By means of the power of the Buddha, the power of samādhi, and the power of one’s own original merit—due to these three factors, one is able to see [the Buddha].

It is like a person who is young and handsome, wearing fine clothes, and wishing to see his own reflection; if he uses a mirror, or sesame oil, or pure water, or crystal to reflect himself, he will see his own form therein.
“Bhadra, do you think that a reflection could possibly enter from the outside into a mirror, sesame oil, water,
or crystal? Bhadra replied, “No, it could not.”
O God among Gods!
It is because the mirror, sesame oil, water, and crystal are pure that one sees their own reflection therein!
The reflection does not emerge from within, nor does it enter from without.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Bhadrapāla!"
Because form is pure, all that exists is pure.
Whenever he wished to see the Buddha, he saw him; whenever he saw him, he questioned him; and whenever he questioned him, he received an answer.
Hearing the sutras, he was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"From where does the Buddha come?
To what place have I gone?
He then reflected for himself: "The Buddha has come from nowhere, and I likewise have gone nowhere."
I reflect that the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—these three realms are merely the products of the mind!
What I contemplate, I immediately see.
The mind creates the Buddha; the mind sees itself; the mind is the Buddha-mind, and the Buddha-mind is my own body.

The mind sees the Buddha; the mind does not know itself, nor does the mind see itself. When the mind has conceptualization, it is delusion; when the mind is without conceptualization, that is nirvana.
This dharma is nothing to be delighted in; even if one were to contemplate it, it is merely emptiness, for there is nothing whatsoever.
"When a Bodhisattva abides in samādhi, what they perceive is as follows.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The mind does not know itself; Though there is a mind, it does not see the mind."
When the mind gives rise to conceptualization, it is delusion; no-mind is nirvana.
This dharma is without solidity; it is always established within mindfulness.
For one who perceives emptiness through understanding, there are no thoughts or aspirations whatsoever.
Chapter Three: The Four Matters “Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they swiftly attain this samādhi:
first, that which they believe cannot be destroyed by anyone.”
Second, his diligence is such that none can cause him to retreat.
Third, his wisdom is such that none can equal it.
Fourth, he constantly associates with and serves virtuous teachers.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters by which one quickly attains this samādhi:
first, one must not harbor worldly thoughts for as long as three months, even for the duration of a finger-snap.
Second, he must not sleep for three months, even for as long as a finger-snap.
Third, he must practice walking meditation (caṅkrama) for three months without rest, except during the time immediately before and after his meals.
Fourth, when preaching the sutras for others, one must not expect offerings from them.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four ways to quickly attain this samādhi:
First, to assemble people and lead them to the Buddha's presence;
second, to assemble people and cause them to listen to the sutras;
third, to be free from envy.
Fourth, teaching others to study the Buddha-way.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four other matters by which one quickly attains this samādhi:
First, to create images of the Buddha in order to accomplish this samādhi;
second, to write out this samādhi using fine silk;
third, to teach those who are arrogant and haughty to enter within the Buddha-way.
"Fourth, one constantly protects the Buddha-dharma. These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Always have faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma; with diligent practice, cultivate profound wisdom and understanding.
Widely distribute it for the sake of others, and be careful never to crave offerings.”
With a mind well-liberated, one leaves desire behind; constantly mindful of the Buddha’s majestic virtue, one fully perceives and knows his countless transformations.
Together with the Honored One among Men in the present, one beholds his various marks and signs of excellence.
Golden-hued and free from defilement or outflows,
listen to this Dharma with an undistracted mind; always abandon the practice of indolence,
and harbor no anger or malice toward others.
Be careful not to doubt this sutra, which all Buddhas praise;
always fashion images of the Buddha.
Always teach others to study this Dharma; by practicing thus, one attains samādhi.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Those who wish to study this samādhi should revere their teacher, serve and make offerings to them, and regard them as they would the Buddha."
If one regards a virtuous teacher as not equal to the Buddha, it will be difficult to attain this samādhi.

Once a bodhisattva has respectfully followed a virtuous teacher to learn and attained this samādhi, they stand empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority and, facing east, sees hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and millions of buddhas; they see them all equally throughout the ten directions.

For example, it is like a person who rises at night and observes the stars, which are exceedingly numerous. If a bodhisattva wishes to see all the Buddhas of the present standing before them, they should revere their good teacher and must not look for the teacher’s shortcomings;
they should fully cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and single-minded concentration, and must not be indolent.
**Chapter Four: The Chapter on Parables** The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

“If a bodhisattva attains this samādhi but does not practice with diligent application, it is like a person who loads a ship full of precious jewels to cross the great ocean, yet the ship breaks apart midway; the people of Jambudvīpa all fall into great sorrow and anxiety, thinking, ‘We have lost all those treasures!’”
When the Bodhisattvas hear of this samādhi and do not study it, all the devas and people will grieve and say with sorrow:
"We have lost such a treasure of sutras!"
The Buddha said:
"This Sūtra of Samādhi is what the Buddha has entrusted and what the Buddha has extolled.
To hear this profound samādhi and yet not write it down, study it, recite it, or maintain it according to the Dharma—this is to be called foolishness."
It is like a foolish son to whom someone brings sandalwood incense and offers it to him, yet he refuses to accept it, calling it impure.
The owner of the incense says:
"This is sandalwood incense; do not call it impure."
"By smelling it one knows its fragrance; by seeing it one knows its purity.
The person closed his eyes, neither smelling nor looking at it.
The Buddha said:
“Those who hear this samādhi and are unwilling to accept and uphold it are like that foolish son; they are ignorant.

They conversely claim that the world exists, failing to enter into emptiness and failing to understand non-existence. Claiming for themselves to be in accord with the Dharma, they instead utter words of frivolous derision:
‘Does the Buddha even have profound sutras?’”
"Does he also possess majestic spiritual power?
they asked, comparing him to one another:
"Is there any other bhikṣu in the world like Ānanda?"
The Buddha said:
"Those people who follow one who maintains this samādhi will go about in pairs or groups of three, speaking with one another:
'What kind of teaching is this? "
"From where did you obtain these words?
You have composed this sutra yourself; it was not spoken by the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"It is, for example, like a merchant who takes a maṇi jewel and shows it to a foolish son of a farmer, saying:
'Appraise this;
what is its value in coins?'"
The merchant said,
"If one takes this jewel and places it in the darkness, the light it illuminates is equal in value to the jewels that fill the entire space.
The Buddha said:
That person, not knowing it was a jewel, said:
"Is its price equal to that of a single ox?
It would be well if you could trade one ox for me; if you are unwilling, let it be."
“In this way, Bhadrapāla!
A bodhisattva who hears of this samādhi and does not believe it, but instead manifests contrary characteristics, is like that foolish son.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"When a bodhisattva hears this samādhi and believes in it, upholds it, and practices it, they will be protected from all four directions, free from fear, and complete in their observance of the precepts; this is what is meant by being 'sublime and brilliant.'"
"With deep wisdom, you should distribute this teaching to others and instruct them one after another, so that this samādhi may long remain in the world.
The Buddha said:

"Foolish people, having failed to make offerings or cultivate merit in their past lives, instead become arrogant, frequently engaging in slander and jealousy. Because they crave wealth and profit, they seek fame and reputation; they merely delight in noisy talk and do not believe in the profound sutras."

If one hears this samādhi and does not believe it, does not delight in it, and does not study it, but instead slanders this sutra, saying, "This was not spoken by the Buddha," the Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"I now speak thus to you for this reason: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill three thousandfold world-systems with precious jewels and give them as alms, even if they possessed such merit, it would not equal that of one who hears this samādhi and believes and delights in it; the latter's blessing surpasses the former."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"What I have said is not otherwise; it is for this reason that I now speak these words!

If anyone sees doubt regarding my teaching of this samādhi, such a person will, in the future, be excluded from the company of evil teachers; even if they were with a good teacher, their merit would be insufficient to mention."
Such people as these associate with evil teachers; hearing this samādhi, they do not believe it, do not delight in it, and do not study it.
Why is this? Because such persons have encountered few Buddhas and possess little wisdom; therefore, they do not believe.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Should there be anyone who hears this samādhi and does not treat it with contempt or derision, does not slander it, does not doubt it, and neither alternately believes nor disbelieves it, but instead rejoices in it, delights in writing it down, and studies, recites, and upholds it—I shall fully know and perceive them all in advance."
That person has not merely performed meritorious deeds under one or two Buddhas, but has heard this samādhi under a hundred Buddhas.
In future ages, should they hear this samādhi and copy, study, recite, and uphold it for even a single day and night, their merit will be incalculable.
"You shall personally attain the stage of *avaivartika*, and whatever you wish for shall be obtained.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"Listen as I speak a parable."

Suppose someone were to take a single buddha-field and grind it entirely into dust, and then take one particle of that dust and break it down until it is as fine as the dust of a single buddha-field—would the number of these particles not be exceedingly great?
Bhadra said: "Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!"
The Buddha said:

"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who took a single mote of dust and placed it in one buddha-field; and suppose he did this for as many buddha-fields as there are motes of dust, filling them all with precious jewels and offering them all to the Buddhas—the merit and virtue of such an act would be but slight!"
It is not as good as hearing this samādhi, studying, writing, reciting, upholding, explaining it to others, and maintaining it.
If one hears it for even a brief moment, its merit cannot be calculated; how much more so for one who has already attained this samādhi in its full perfection.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“If there is a bodhisattva seeking all virtues, They should explain and practice this samādhi;
If they believe, rejoice in it, recite it, and do not doubt, Their merit and blessings will be without limit.”
If one were to take a world-system like a single Buddha-field, break it all apart until it is reduced to dust,
and then take as many Buddha-fields as exceed that number and fill them with precious jewels to give as a gift;
this would not equal the merit and blessings of one who hears this samādhi, for the latter’s merit surpasses the former gift.
The merit of this analogy is beyond comparison; I entrust it to you all, so you should exhort and instruct others to practice with diligence and vigor, never being indolent.
Whoever recites and upholds this samādhi has already beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas face to face.
Even if there should be the greatest terrors at the end of time, one who maintains this samādhi has nothing to fear.
This bhikṣu who practices it has already seen me; he always follows the Buddha and never departs from him.
"Just as the Buddha has spoken, there is no difference; the Bodhisattva should always follow his teaching, and shall swiftly attain the ocean of wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Chapter Five: The Fourfold Assembly. Vaidhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!"
If there is one who has renounced sensual desires to become a bhikṣu, having heard this samādhi, how should they train?
How should they uphold it?
How should they practice it?
The Buddha said:
“One who has abandoned sensual desires to become a bhikṣu and wishes to study this samādhi must maintain the precepts with purity; they must not be deficient by even a hair’s breadth.”
"One should always stand in awe of the suffering of hell and remain far removed from flattery; this is what constitutes purity.
"What, then, constitutes a deficiency in the precepts?"
The Buddha said:
"One seeks form. [The monk asked:
"In what way does one seek form?"
The Buddha said:
"That person thinks to himself, 'I maintain the precepts and guard myself, so that in a future life I may be reborn as a deva or as a Cakravartin king.'"
"To thus delight in sensual desires is to be deficient in the precepts.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Those who wish to study this samādhi should maintain purity and self-restraint, keeping the precepts perfectly complete; they must not be flatterers or hypocrites, and they should always be praised by the wise."

In the sutras it is said: "One should practice giving and diligence; one's resolve should be firm; one should have great faith and encourage joy; one should serve the teacher as if looking upon them as a Buddha, and thus swiftly attain samādhi."
"If one fails to show reverence and instead treats the teacher with contempt, belittling, or deceiving them, then even if they have studied this samādhi for a long time, they will quickly forget it.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"If a bodhisattva hears this samādhi from a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, they should regard that person as a Buddha and always revere them; they must not harbor a deceitful attitude toward them."
A bodhisattva must not harbor a deceitful mind; they should always be sincere and constantly delight in dwelling in solitude.

They should not begrudge their own body or life, nor should they hope for what others might seek to give them. They should always practice begging for food and not accept invitations, maintaining their own discipline and contentment with whatever is obtained.
"One should not lie down in indolence while practicing walking meditation; such is the instruction in the sutras.
One who studies this samādhi should maintain it in this manner.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is difficult to fathom, O God among Gods!
If in a future age there should be indolent bodhisattvas who, upon hearing of this samādhi, are unwilling to apply themselves with diligence and study it, what should be done?”
"If there are bodhisattvas who, with diligent effort, wish to study this, we shall follow the teachings of this sutra.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Bhadrapāla!"
I rejoice in this; the Buddhas of the past, future, and present all likewise rejoice.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Uphold everything as I have taught it; Always dwell alone and practice meritorious deeds."
Maintaining one’s own discipline and not gathering in assemblies, Constantly practicing alms-gathering and not accepting invitations;
Revering the Dharma Master as if he were the Buddha, Eliminating sleepiness and resolving to attain liberation;
Always being diligent and never indolent— A practitioner who acts in this way shall attain samādhi.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bhikṣuṇī seeks the bodhisattva path and wishes to study this samādhi, how should she practice?
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣuṇīs who seek this samādhi must not be self-exalting, but should always be humble and modest.
They must not be self-important, nor arrogant; they must not be envious, nor wrathful; they must not covet wealth, profit, or sensual pleasures.”

One should always remain pure and must not begrudge one's own body or life; one should always delight in the sutras and Dharma, cherishing extensive learning, and should abandon lust, anger, and delusion. One must not covet fine clothing, pearls, or ornaments, but should instead be praised by the wise.
One should revere a good teacher as if they were a Buddha, never harboring any insincere or flattering thoughts.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“If a bhikṣuṇī seeks samādhi, She should always be diligent and never indolent.
She must not yield to a mind of greed and desire, And she should eliminate anger and self-importance.”
One must not be arrogant, deceitful, or frivolous; one should always practice with utmost sincerity and establish single-minded faith.
One should revere the virtuous teacher as if they were a Buddha; a practitioner who acts in this way shall attain samādhi.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there is a layperson practicing the Way who hears of this samādhi and wishes to study it, how should they practice?
The Buddha said:
“Householder, one who wishes to study this samādhi should uphold the five precepts with firm resolve:
one must not drink alcohol, nor cause others to drink;

one must not become intimate with women, nor teach others to do so; one must harbor no affection for wife, children, or grandchildren; one must not covet wealth or property; and one should constantly keep in mind the desire to renounce the household life and become a śramaṇa.”
One should constantly observe the eightfold precepts within a Buddhist monastery;
one should always practice giving, yet after having given, one should not think, "I shall personally obtain its merit," but rather give for the sake of all beings.
One should always maintain great compassion and reverence for one's virtuous teachers;
upon seeing a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, one must not lightly speak of his faults.
Having practiced in this way, one should study and maintain this samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If a householder wishes to study this samādhi, He should uphold the five precepts without violation or deficiency.
He should constantly intend to become a śramaṇa, And not covet wife, children, wealth, or sensual pleasures."
Constantly observe the eightfold precepts at Buddhist temples; do not be arrogant or treat others with contempt.
Let your mind be free from the hope for glory or the pursuit of desires; practice the teachings of the sutras with a heart free from flattery.
Abandon stinginess and greed, always practicing generous giving; one should always revere and honor the community of bhikṣus.
"Always set your mind on the single practice and do not be indolent; those who study this samādhi should act in this way.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If upāsikās hear of this samādhi and wish to study it, how should they practice?"
The Buddha said:
"If a laywoman wishes to study, she should uphold the five precepts and take refuge in the Three.
What are these three?"
Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
One must not serve other paths, must not prostrate to heavenly deities, must not offer sacrifices to spirits or ghosts, and must not observe auspicious or favorable days.
One must not engage in frivolous play, nor be arrogant or self-indulgent regarding perceptions of form, nor harbor a mind of greedy desire.

One should always be mindful of giving, take joy in desiring to hear the sutras, apply the power of mindfulness to study, and revere virtuous teachers; the mind should always remain earnest and never succumb to indolence.
"If there be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who exceed [the limit], they shall be provided with seats and guest-food.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The upāsikā who wishes to study samādhi Should uphold the five precepts without deficiency or violation."
Serve the virtuous teacher as you would the Buddha; do not prostrate to celestial shrines or worship spirits.
Abandon killing, stealing, and envy; do not engage in double-tongued speech to incite strife between others.
Do not be stingy or greedy, but always contemplate giving; when seeing evil, conceal it and speak only of the good.
One must not be sycophantic or engage in sexual misconduct; one should always be humble and never arrogant.
By reverently serving bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, one who practices in this way attains samādhi.

Chapter Six: On Protection. The eight bodhisattvas—Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Guhagupta, Naradatta, Susīma, Mahāsusārthavāha, Indradatta, and Varuṇadeva—seeing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly delighted. They offered five hundred garments of *kāyapa* cloth as a gift, surrendered their own bodies in refuge, and made offerings of precious jewels.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Bhadra and the other five hundred people are teachers among men; they constantly uphold the True Dharma and teach in accordance with it, so that all rejoice. Those who delight in attending them have pure minds free from desire."
At that time, the five hundred people all stood before the Buddha with their palms joined.
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By maintaining how many practices does a bodhisattva swiftly attain this samādhi?"
The Buddha said:
"There are four things:
first, not believing in other paths."
Second, severing craving and desire.
Third, practicing pure conduct.
Fourth, being free from greed.
These are the four.
A practitioner who acts in this way will obtain five hundred merits in this very life.
For example, a bhikṣu with a mind of loving-kindness will never be harmed by poison, weapons cannot strike him, fire cannot burn him, and he will not drown or be injured when entering water.
Even when the kalpa comes to an end in flames, one who falls into this fire will find the fire extinguished, just as a great flood extinguishes a small fire.

For a bodhisattva who maintains this samādhi, whether it be emperors, thieves, water or fire, dragons, yakṣas, pythons, lions, tigers, wolves, monkeys, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, or any venomous beasts and spirits that wish to harass people, kill people, seize their robes and bowls, destroy their meditation, or steal their mindfulness—none can ever succeed in harming such a bodhisattva.
"Except for the consequences of their past karma which cannot be avoided, it will be no different from what I have said.

The Buddha said, "Those who uphold this samādhi shall never suffer pain in their eyes, nor in their ears, nose, mouth, or body; their minds shall never be troubled, except for that which was produced by their past karma."
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva is praised by all the devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and by humans and non-humans alike;
they all together protect, serve, and make offerings to them, looking upon them with reverence and longing to see them. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do likewise."
Whatever sutras this bodhisattva has not yet recited and has not previously heard or retained, he shall obtain them all through the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi.
If he does not obtain them during the day, he shall obtain them all within his dreams at night.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"If there were those who uphold this samādhi, I could describe their merits for one kalpa and even beyond another kalpa without reaching their end; I have merely stated the essentials here."
Chapter Seven: Encouragement and Assistance. The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"Within this samādhi, there are four matters that assist a bodhisattva in generating joy."
The Buddhas of the past maintained this samādhi, and by means of it, they assisted their joy and personally attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, becoming fully endowed with all wisdom.
The countless Buddhas currently existing throughout the ten directions likewise obtain [the merit] through these four ways of rejoicing within this samādhi;
those yet to come shall also obtain it through these four ways of rejoicing, and I rejoice in them all.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"In this samādhi, there are four matters that assist in generating joy; I shall now provide a brief analogy for them.
Suppose a person were to travel across the earth for a hundred years without ceasing, their pace surpassing even the swift wind—would anyone be able to calculate the distance of their journey?"
Bhadra said: "There is no one capable of calculating it.
Only the Buddha’s disciple Śāriputra and the avaivartika bodhisattvas are able to calculate it."
The Buddha said:

"I therefore tell all bodhisattvas: if there are good men or good women who take the place where this person practices and fill it with precious jewels to offer in charity, it would not equal the merit of hearing this samādhi and rejoicing in its four aspects. The latter's merit exceeds that of the former by hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis."
"You should know that this merit which assists in rejoicing is exceedingly sublime and vast.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"In the distant past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Śikhin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, who dwelt in a secluded place."

At that time, Jambudvīpa was eighteen hundred thousand *koṭis* of *li* in length and breadth; it contained six million four hundred thousand kingdoms, all of which were abundant and fertile, with a flourishing population.

There was a great kingdom named Bhadraha, where a wheel-turning monarch named Vessika resided. He went to the place where the Buddha was, and after performing his prostrations, withdrew to sit to one side.
Knowing his thoughts, the Buddha then preached this samādhi for him.
Upon hearing this, the king rejoiced greatly; he immediately took precious jewels and scattered them over the Buddha, thinking to himself:
"By means of these merits, may all the people of the ten directions attain peace and security."
At that time, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Sihakṣatra, King Viśvantara reached the end of his life and was reborn in his own family as a crown prince named Brahmadatta.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ratna who preached this samādhi for the fourfold assembly of disciples.

When Brahmādamitra heard it, he rejoiced with great joy; leaping up, he scattered jewels worth ten billion over him and further offered fine robes as an act of worship. Having resolved his mind to seek the Buddha-way, he went together with a thousand people to become śramaṇas under this bhikṣu, seeking to study this samādhi. Together with those thousand people, they served their teacher for eight thousand years without weariness or indolence.
Having once heard this samādhi and being aided by these four matters, they enter high and clear wisdom.

Because of this, they shall later behold sixty-eight thousand Buddhas; at the abode of each and every Buddha, they hear this samādhi and personally attain Buddhahood, receiving the names Tīrṇavīra (坻羅惟逮), Samyaksaṃbuddha (等正覺), Anuttarapuruṣa (無上士), Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām (道法御), Buddha, and Bhagavat (佛、世尊).
At that time, there were one thousand bhikṣus who had attained equal and right enlightenment, all named Tiroyaśas.
They taught immeasurable people so that they all sought the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"Who would hear of this samādhi and not rejoice, study, uphold, recite, and explain it to others?
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who uphold this samādhi, they will swiftly attain Buddhahood; yet even merely hearing of its merit is immeasurable, let alone those who study and uphold it."
If one must travel a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek this samādhi, how much more so should one seek and study it when it is near at hand?

If there is anyone who hears of this samādhi and wishes to learn it, they should serve their teacher for ten years, providing offerings and looking after them without acting according to their own will; they should follow the teacher’s instructions and constantly mind the teacher’s kindness.
The Buddha said:
"I shall therefore explain this to you.
If one hears of this samādhi even from four thousand li away and goes to that place, even if they do not actually hear it, their merit will be incalculable."
Why is this? Because through single-minded diligence, one will certainly attain it and personally realize Buddhahood.
Chapter Eight: On Sincerity. The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Satyanāman, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Anuttara, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Varuṇa who, after that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, upheld this samādhi."

At that time, I was a king of the Kṣatriya caste. In a dream, I heard of this samādhi; upon waking, I immediately set out to seek that bhikṣu. I then became a śramaṇa under his guidance, desiring to hear this samādhi. I served my teacher for thirty-six thousand years, yet because demonic obstacles arose repeatedly, I was ultimately unable to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās:

"I tell you this for a reason: you must quickly take up this samādhi and not allow it to be forgotten. Serve your teacher well and maintain this samādhi for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or even a hundred thousand kalpas, without ever becoming weary."
One should never leave one's virtuous teacher. Regarding food, drink, and necessities—clothing, bedding, and even precious treasures—one should not harbor any sense of stinginess or attachment.

Should these be lacking, one must go out to beg for alms to provide for the teacher. One should strive to attain this samādhi without weariness; one should constantly be willing to cut off one's own flesh to offer it to the virtuous teacher, let alone material wealth, which hardly needs mentioning!
One should serve a virtuous teacher just as a servant serves his master; one who seeks this samādhi should act in this manner.
Having attained the samādhi, one should firmly maintain it and constantly remember the teacher’s kindness.

This samādhi is difficult to encounter; even if one were to seek this samādhi for as many as a hundred thousand kalpas, it would be impossible even to hear its name, let alone study it without being diligent.

If one attains this samādhi and studies it with diligence to teach and transform others, even if one were to give away as many precious jewels as would fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such vast generosity would not equal the merit of studying this samādhi.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"If there are those who wish to study this, they should rejoice in support of it; those who wish to study shall attain it. Those who study do so through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, which enables their learning. They should carefully transcribe this samādhi upon silk, seal it with the seal of the Buddha, and provide it with excellent offerings."
What is called the Buddha-seal? It is said:

that which is not to be practiced; that which is without greed, without seeking, without conceptualization, without attachment, without aspiration, without inclination toward rebirth, without grasping, without looking back, without dwelling, without obstruction, without fetters, and without anything at all; the exhaustion of desire; that which is without arising, without ceasing, without destruction, and without decay—the essential path and the fundamental nature of the path are the seal.
"It is that which even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas cannot attain, let alone those who are ignorant and deluded.
This seal is the Buddha-seal.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"When I now preached this samādhi, one thousand eight hundred billion devas, asuras, ghosts and spirits, nāgas, and human beings attained the stage of srotāpanna;
eight hundred bhikṣus attained arhatship;
and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained arhatship."
Ten thousand bodhisattvas attained this samādhi and, having realized the dharma of non-arising, stood therein;
twelve thousand bodhisattvas no longer regressed.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Bhadrapāla, and the others:

"I have sought the Way for incalculable kalpas and have now attained Buddhahood; I entrust this sutra to you all, so that you may study, recite, uphold, and preserve it without ever forgetting or losing it."
"If there are those who wish to study this, you should fully and calmly instruct them.
To those who wish to hear it, you should explain it fully.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and his companions, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Ānanda, as well as the devas, asuras, nāgas, spirits, and humans, were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha
